{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_015gKeeK2B5xjcGe8s9ytgRF","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections below in this order. Headings may be renamed slightly to suit the domain, but keep the order and intent. For small systems, a section may be a single sentence. If a section does not apply, keep its heading and give a one-line reason. Prefer tables where the notes suggest them.\n4\t\n5\t---\n6\t\n7\t## 1. Summary\n8\t\n9\tFive to ten sentences or a tight bullet list covering:\n10\t\n11\t- What is being built and for whom.\n12\t- The overall shape of the architecture in one or two sentences.\n13\t- The three to five most important decisions.\n14\t- What the first milestone delivers.\n15\t- The top risks.\n16\t\n17\tSomeone who reads only this section should know what is about to happen and why.\n18\t\n19\t## 2. Context and Goals\n20\t\n21\t- **Problem:** what is painful or missing today, and for whom.\n22\t- **Goals:** the outcomes the system must achieve, in measurable terms where possible.\n23\t- **Non-goals:** things deliberately left out of scope, so nobody assumes they are coming.\n24\t- **Success measures:** how you will know it worked after launch, such as adoption, latency, cost, accuracy, or time saved.\n25\t\n26\t## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n27\t\n28\t- **Ranked quality attributes:** a table with the columns *attribute*, *measurable target*, and *why it matters*, in priority order. Mark targets you inferred as assumptions.\n29\t- **Key functional requirements:** the capabilities that shape the structure. This is not a full backlog.\n30\t- **Constraints:** existing stack, hosting, team size and skills, deadline, budget, compliance, data residency, and mandated vendors.\n31\t- **Hard parts:** the few areas that are new, uncertain, dependent on outside parties, or costly to get wrong, each with one sentence on why.\n32\t\n33\t## 4. Current State\n34\t\n35\tWhat exists today that this work touches: relevant code, services, data stores, infrastructure, and processes. Cite specific files, modules, or systems where you inspected them. Note conventions the plan will follow. For entirely new builds, state what organisational or platform context applies.\n36\t\n37\t## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n38\t\n39\t- **Assumptions:** a table with the columns *assumption*, *impact if wrong*, and *how and when it will be validated*.\n40\t- **Open questions:** each with the owner or person who can answer it, the default you will use if no answer arrives, and the date or milestone by which it must be resolved.\n41\t\n42\t## 6. Architecture Overview\n43\t\n44\t- A text-based diagram (Mermaid or ASCII) showing components, data stores, external systems, and trust boundaries.\n45\t- A short narrative of how the parts fit together.\n46\t- A **component table** with the columns *component*, *responsibility*, *owns which data*, *exposes which interfaces*, *technology*, and *key dependencies*.\n47\t\n48\t## 7. Component Details\n49\t\n50\tFor each significant component:\n51\t\n52\t- Its responsibility and its boundaries, meaning what it explicitly does not do.\n53\t- Its interfaces: whether they are synchronous or asynchronous, the contract format, how they are versioned, and the expected load.\n54\t- Its internal structure, where that matters.\n55\t- How it fails and how it recovers.\n56\t- How it scales, if scale is a driver.\n57\t\n58\tRoutine components can be covered in a line or two.\n59\t\n60\t## 8. Data Design\n61\t\n62\t- The main entities and how they relate to each other.\n63\t- The system of record for each entity, and which component writes to it.\n64\t- Consistency requirements and where transactions are needed.\n65\t- Access patterns and the indexing or partitioning they imply.\n66\t- Retention, deletion, backup, and restore targets.\n67\t- Data classification, covering sensitive fields and how they are protected.\n68\t- How schemas will evolve and how migrations will be done.\n69\t\n70\t## 9. Key Flows\n71\t\n72\tWalk through the two to four most important scenarios step by step, from trigger to outcome. Use sequence diagrams or numbered steps. Include at least one failure path, such as a timeout, retry, duplicate, partial failure, or dependency outage, and show how the system behaves.\n73\t\n74\t## 10. Key Decisions\n75\t\n76\tOne entry per significant decision, optionally as a table:\n77\t\n78\t- **Decision:** what was decided.\n79\t- **Options considered:** at least two realistic ones.\n80\t- **Rationale:** why this option, measured against the ranked drivers.\n81\t- **Reversibility:** whether it is hard or easy to undo.\n82\t- **Revisit if:** the evidence or condition that would reopen the decision.\n83\t\n84\t## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n85\t\n86\tA short subsection for each. Name the concrete mechanism and the milestone in which it is built.\n87\t\n88\t- **Security:** identity, authorisation model, secrets, encryption, input validation, the main threats and their mitigations.\n89\t- **Reliability:** availability and recovery targets, redundancy, timeouts, retries, idempotency, backpressure.\n90\t- **Observability:** logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts tied to user-facing symptoms.\n91\t- **Performance and capacity:** expected load, the bottlenecks you expect, and how they will be load-tested.\n92\t- **Cost:** estimated run cost, the main cost drivers, and the controls on spend.\n93\t- **Operations:** who owns the system, runbooks, on-call expectations, and how support works.\n94\t- **AI-specific concerns, where relevant:** evaluation approach, guardrails, cost and latency budgets, human approval points, and the fallback when the model fails.\n95\t\n96\t## 12. Build Sequence\n97\t\n98\tA milestone table or list. For each milestone:\n99\t\n100\t- **Goal:** the risk it clears or the value it delivers.\n101\t- **Scope:** what is included and what is explicitly excluded.\n102\t- **Deliverables:** the concrete artefacts, features, or environments it produces.\n103\t- **Exit criteria:** checkable conditions that mark it complete.\n104\t- **Dependencies:** what must be finished first, and what can run in parallel.\n105\t- **Rough size:** a range, with the team assumption behind it.\n106\t\n107\tThe first milestone must contain a thin end-to-end slice and the spikes for the highest-risk unknowns. Mark the critical path.\n108\t\n109\t## 13. First Milestone Task Breakdown\n110\t\n111\tA list of concrete tasks. Each one has a verb and a deliverable, its location (module, directory, service, or repository), and a \"done when\" condition. Note the order and which tasks can run in parallel. Spikes include the question being answered, a time box, and the result that would change the plan.\n112\t\n113\t## 14. Testing and Validation Strategy\n114\t\n115\t- Which kinds of tests cover which risks: unit, contract, integration, end-to-end, load, security, and evaluation sets for AI components.\n116\t- The test environments and test data needed.\n117\t- What runs in CI and what blocks a release.\n118\t- How the measurable targets in Section 3 will actually be verified.\n119\t\n120\t## 15. Rollout, Migration, and Rollback\n121\t\n122\t- How the system reaches users: feature flags, staged or percentage rollout, beta groups.\n123\t- For changes to existing systems: how old and new run side by side, the steps for migrating data, and the switchover criteria.\n124\t- The rollback procedure for each risky step, and the point after which rolling back is no longer possible.\n125\t\n126\t## 16. Risks and Mitigations\n127\t\n128\tA table with the columns *risk*, *likelihood*, *impact*, *mitigation*, *early warning sign*, and *owner*. Include technical, delivery, dependency, and organisational risks.\n129\t\n130\t## 17. Deferred Work and Future Evolution\n131\t\n132\t- Items deliberately postponed, and what would trigger building each one.\n133\t- Ways the architecture is expected to evolve, and the extension points that support it.\n134\t- Known shortcuts or technical debt taken on purpose, with a plan to pay each one back.\n135\t\n136\t## 18. Next Steps\n137\t\n138\tThree to seven actions someone can take immediately. These include answering the open questions that block progress and starting the first tasks. Name the specific files, commands, or people where possible.\n139\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"aaba8a00-b2f7-41a1-a0f7-e2835438b137","uuid":"84d1568a-f503-447f-aabc-751af9c8c863","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:05:49.396Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p2ab33809\\skills\\architecture-planner\\reference\\document-template.md","content":"# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n\nUse the sections below in this order. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01U66QsCdjUMgWvpdt79pYST","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections that are relevant. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n4\t\n5\t## 1. Discovery questions\n6\t\n7\tChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n8\t\n9\t- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n10\t- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n11\t- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n12\t- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n13\t- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n14\t- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n15\t- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n16\t- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n17\t- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n18\t- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n19\t\n20\t## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n21\t\n22\t| Attribute | Express it as |\n23\t|---|---|\n24\t| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n25\t| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n26\t| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n27\t| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n28\t| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n29\t| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n30\t| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n31\t| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n32\t| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n33\t\n34\tIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n35\t\n36\t## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n37\t\n38\t- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n39\t- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n40\t- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n41\t- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n42\t- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n43\t- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n44\t- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n45\t\n46\t## 4. Data checklist\n47\t\n48\t- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n49\t- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n50\t- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n51\t- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n52\t- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n53\t- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n54\t- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n55\t- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n56\t\n57\t## 5. Choosing technology\n58\t\n59\t- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n60\t- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n61\t- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n62\t- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n63\t- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n64\t- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n65\t\n66\t## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n67\t\n68\t- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n69\t- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n70\t- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n71\t- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n72\t- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n73\t- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n74\t- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n75\t\n76\t## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n77\t\n78\tA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n79\t\n80\t- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n81\t- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n82\t- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n83\t- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n84\t\n85\tKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n86\t\n87\t## 8. Security checklist\n88\t\n89\t- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n90\t- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n91\t- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n92\t- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n93\t- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n94\t- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n95\t- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n96\t- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n97\t- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n98\t\n99\t## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n100\t\n101\t- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n102\t- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n103\t- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n104\t- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n105\t- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n106\t- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n107\t- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n108\t- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n109\t- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n110\t\n111\t## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n112\t\n113\t- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n114\t- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n115\t- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n116\t- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n117\t- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n118\t- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n119\t- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n120\t- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n121\t- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n122\t- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n123\t- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Sample production traffic back into the evaluation set.\n124\t- **Data handling:** what is sent to model providers, how long they keep it, and whether it is allowed to be sent.\n125\t\n126\t## 11. Infrastructure checklist\n127\t\n128\t- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n129\t- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n130\t- Remote infrastructure state with locking. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n131\t- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n132\t- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n133\t- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n134\t- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n135\t- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n136\t\n137\t## 12. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n145\t\n146\t## 13. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n\n## 1. Discovery questions\n\nChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n\n- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n\n## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n\n| Attribute | Express it as |\n|---|---|\n| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n\nIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n\n## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n\n- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n\n## 4. Data checklist\n\n- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n\n## 5. Choosing technology\n\n- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n\n## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n\n- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n\n## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n\nA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n\n- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n\nKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n\n## 8. Security checklist\n\n- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n\n## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n\n- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n\n## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n\n- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Sample production traffic back into the evaluation set.\n- **Data handling:** what is sent to model providers, how long they keep it, and whether it is allowed to be sent.\n\n## 11. Infrastructure checklist\n\n- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n- Remote infrastructure state with locking. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n\n## 12. Brownfield and migration checklist\n\n- List what the current system actually does, including undocumented behaviour that users rely on.\n- Find a point where requests or data can be split between the old and new systems.\n- Decide whether to migrate incrementally, by feature, tenant, or traffic percentage, or all at once, and justify the choice.\n- Plan how data stays in sync while both systems run, and how the two will be reconciled.\n- Define switchover criteria and the point after which rollback is no longer possible.\n- Plan when the old system will be retired. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n\n## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n\n- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n","numLines":157,"startLine":1,"totalLines":157}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_oi3byn7iux2hfu35rs6hzfgwar7aygv2dk43wirglxpiscfolxya","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# Build plan: real-time collaborative document editor\n\n> **Context.** The workspace has no code (its `README.md` says it is intentionally empty), and the request gave no scale, team, stack or compliance details. I didn't stop to ask. I wrote down assumptions, labelled **A1–A10**, and the plan rests on them. You asked about build order, so Sections 12–13 have the most detail. The other sections are short but complete.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** A browser-based rich-text editor where business teams edit the same document at the same time. It shows live cursors, has sharing permissions, comments and version history, and keeps working through short network drops. Think of a focused Google Docs for teams (A1).\n- **Shape:** A React and TipTap editor in the browser. A **`collab`** WebSocket service, built on the open-source Yjs ecosystem (Hocuspocus), merges and relays edits. A separate **`api`** service handles login, documents, sharing and comments. Both store data in one Postgres database. Everything runs on AWS ECS Fargate.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Edits are merged with a **CRDT (Yjs)**, not operational transformation. A CRDT is a data structure that lets copies edited separately merge automatically and end up identical.\n  2. We build on **open-source Yjs, TipTap and Hocuspocus** instead of buying a managed collaboration service or writing a sync server from scratch.\n  3. Documents are stored as an **append-only log of updates plus a compacted snapshot in Postgres**. Multiple servers can write to it safely.\n  4. **\"Saved\" is a real guarantee.** The server tells each client which of its edits are committed to the database.\n  5. **Two deployables, `api` and `collab`,** so that releasing the API doesn't disconnect everyone who is editing.\n- **First milestone (about 4–5 weeks):** Two people log in and edit the same document in a deployed staging environment. Their edits survive a server crash. Three time-boxed spikes run in parallel: editor binding and merge correctness, the durability and \"Saved\" guarantee, and WebSocket behaviour on AWS.\n- **Top risks:**\n  - Silent data loss or copies that drift apart. This is the worst outcome possible.\n  - Changes to the document schema deleting content on older clients.\n  - Permission checks being skipped on the WebSocket path.\n  - The team's lack of CRDT experience slowing everything down.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Teams now draft in files they email around or in tools that lock a document to one editor. Concurrent edits collide or overwrite each other, and nobody can trust which copy is current.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Several people edit one document at once and see each other's changes in under 250 ms.\n  - No edit the UI reported as saved is ever lost.\n  - Access control is enforced on every path.\n  - Private beta in about 16 weeks (A5).\n- **Non-goals for beta:** spreadsheets and slides, native mobile apps, full offline-first use (creating or browsing documents offline), suggestion or track-changes mode, public link sharing, SAML/SCIM, import and export, search, AI features, multi-region, end-to-end encryption.\n- **Success measures:**\n  - At least 5 beta workspaces active weekly.\n  - Zero confirmed lost-edit incidents.\n  - p95 time for an edit to reach other editors under 250 ms, measured in production by a synthetic probe.\n  - At least 99.9% of minutes with the editing service available.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | **Data integrity** | (a) All clients and the stored copy are byte-identical after merging, with 0 drift across 10,000 fuzz runs per night. (b) Recovery point is zero for any edit the UI showed as \"Saved\". (c) \"Saved\" appears within 2 s at p95 after typing stops. *(Assumption)* | Losing someone's writing destroys trust and can't be repaired afterwards. |\n| 2 | **Access-control correctness** | No read or write without permission, checked on HTTP and WebSocket paths. Revoked access takes effect on live sessions within 5 s. *(Assumption)* | Documents hold business-confidential content (A6). |\n| 3 | **Collaboration latency** | Local keystroke to screen under 16 ms and never waits on the network. Remote edit propagation under 250 ms p95 in-region, for documents with up to 20 editors. *(Assumption)* | This is what makes it feel \"real-time\". |\n| 4 | **Time to market** | Private beta in about 16 weeks with 5 engineers (A3, A5). | Rules out building merge algorithms from scratch. |\n| 5 | **Availability** | Editing available 99.9% monthly. A deploy or crash causes at most about 5 s of reconnecting and loses no edits. If `collab` goes down, users keep typing locally. *(Assumption)* | A CRDT lets us trade server uptime for client resilience. |\n\nCost comes after these. The target is under about $1,000/month at beta scale *(assumption)*.\n\n**Key functional requirements that shape the structure:**\n- Rich text: headings, lists, bold/italic/code, links, images, block quotes. Tables are a stretch goal.\n- Live presence and cursors.\n- Per-document roles: owner, editor, commenter, viewer.\n- Comments anchored to text.\n- Version history with restore.\n- Edits made during a disconnect sync when the connection returns.\n\n**Constraints (all assumed):**\n- 5 engineers who are strong in TypeScript, React, Node and Postgres, with no CRDT experience (A3).\n- AWS, single region (A4).\n- No regulated data (A6).\n- Managed OIDC identity (A8).\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n| Hard part | Why it's hard |\n|---|---|\n| H1. Merge correctness and editor binding | New to the team. Bugs show up as rare divergence that is hard to reproduce. |\n| H2. Durability and \"Saved\" semantics | Yjs servers usually persist on a debounce, so a crash can lose the last few seconds unless the design closes that gap. |\n| H3. Authorisation on long-lived WebSockets | Permissions change while connections stay open. Viewers must not be able to send edits even from a modified client. |\n| H4. Document schema evolution | The document format is effectively permanent. y-prosemirror can **delete** content it can't map to an older client's schema *(to verify in S1)*. |\n| H5. Running more than one `collab` instance | Fan-out between instances, multiple writers to the same document, compaction, and reconnect storms during deploys. |\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nThe workspace is empty: no code, infrastructure, CI or data. No organisational platform, mandated vendors or existing identity provider were mentioned, so the plan uses AWS and managed services (A4, A8). It proposes this repository layout:\n\n```\napps/web            React + Vite + TipTap client\napps/api            Fastify HTTP API\napps/collab         Hocuspocus WebSocket server\npackages/doc-schema shared TipTap/ProseMirror schema + schema_version (used by web AND collab)\npackages/protocol   shared types: collab-token claims, stateless message types\ndb/migrations       SQL migrations (node-pg-migrate)\ninfra/terraform     modules/ + envs/staging, envs/prod\ntests/fuzz, tests/e2e (Playwright), tests/load\ndocs/adr            decision records\n```\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n**Assumptions**\n\n| ID | Assumption | Impact if wrong | How and when validated |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| A1 | B2B product. A workspace is the tenant boundary. One shared database with `workspace_id` on every row. | Consumer or public scale changes capacity, abuse and sharing models. | Product owner, week 1 |\n| A2 | Up to 10k MAU, 1,000 documents open at once, 3,000 WebSocket connections. Usually 1–5 editors per document, capped at 50. | Higher scale brings doc-affinity routing and DB partitioning forward. | Product owner, week 1. Load test in M3 at 2×. |\n| A3 | 5 engineers, strong in TypeScript and Node, new to CRDTs | Sizes are off. The buy option becomes more attractive. | Eng manager, week 1 |\n| A4 | AWS, one region, no mandated stack | Swap ECS, RDS and Cognito for equivalents. The architecture stays the same. | Week 1 |\n| A5 | Beta target about 16 weeks, no hard external date | Scope cuts come from Section 17. | Week 1 |\n| A6 | Business-confidential data only. No HIPAA or PCI, no residency rules, no E2E encryption. | E2E encryption rules out server-side merging, snapshots and comments as designed. | Week 1 |\n| A7 | \"Offline\" means surviving minutes to hours of disconnect in an open tab, plus tab close via IndexedDB | Full offline-first means extra work on local document lists and conflict UX. | Product owner, week 1 |\n| A8 | Cognito with email and Google sign-in. SAML deferred. | Enterprise SSO for beta adds about 1–2 weeks. | Week 1 |\n| A9 | 95% of documents under 50 pages. Hard limit 10 MB encoded (about 200 pages). | Large documents need lazy loading. | S1 measures load time. |\n| A10 | MIT-licensed OSS (Yjs, TipTap core, Hocuspocus) is acceptable | Licence review could force a different editor. | Legal, week 1 |\n\n**Open questions**\n\n| Question | Owner | Default if no answer | Needed by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Would you pay for a managed collaboration service (e.g. Liveblocks or Tiptap Cloud) to save about 4–6 weeks? | Product/finance | No. Build on OSS (D2). | End of S1 (week 2) |\n| Is suggestion or track-changes mode needed for beta? | Product | No | Before M2 schema freeze (week 6) |\n| Are tables needed for beta? | Product | Stretch goal in M3 | Week 6 |\n| Is enterprise SSO needed for beta tenants? | Sales | No | Week 8 |\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  subgraph Browser[\"Browser (untrusted)\"]\n    W[web: React + TipTap + Yjs<br/>y-indexeddb local cache]\n  end\n  subgraph AWS[\"AWS VPC (trusted)\"]\n    CF[CloudFront + S3<br/>static web, image assets]\n    ALB[ALB: HTTPS + WSS]\n    API[api: Fastify<br/>ECS Fargate x2]\n    COL[collab: Hocuspocus<br/>ECS Fargate x2+]\n    PG[(Postgres RDS Multi-AZ<br/>metadata, ACL, doc_updates,<br/>doc_snapshots, versions, comments)]\n    RD[(Redis ElastiCache<br/>cross-instance fan-out, M3)]\n    SM[Secrets Manager<br/>collab-token signing key]\n  end\n  COG[Cognito OIDC]\n\n  W -- HTTPS --> CF\n  W -- HTTPS REST --> ALB --> API\n  W -- WSS Yjs sync + awareness --> ALB --> COL\n  W -- OIDC --> COG\n  API -- verify session --> COG\n  API --> PG\n  API -- NOTIFY acl_changed --> PG\n  COL -- LISTEN acl_changed / load / append / compact --> PG\n  COL <--> RD\n  API & COL --> SM\n  API -- presigned upload URLs --> CF\n```\n\n**How the parts fit together.**\n\nThe browser keeps a full Yjs copy of each open document. Typing changes the local copy straight away and gets saved to IndexedDB. The resulting update goes over a WebSocket to `collab`.\n\n`collab` does five things:\n- applies the update to its in-memory copy of the document;\n- relays it to other connected editors, and to other `collab` instances through Redis;\n- appends merged batches to `doc_updates` in Postgres every 500 ms;\n- tells clients which state is now committed;\n- compacts the log into a snapshot from time to time.\n\n`api` owns everything that isn't document content: users, workspaces, documents, permissions, comments, versions and uploads. It also issues short-lived **collab tokens**, which `collab` checks when a client connects. Permission changes reach live connections through Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`.\n\n**Component table**\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns (writes) | Exposes | Technology | Key dependencies |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `web` | Editing UI, local merging, offline cache, presence display | IndexedDB cache (client) | none | React, Vite, TipTap, Yjs, y-indexeddb, HocuspocusProvider | `api`, `collab`, Cognito |\n| `api` | Auth sessions, workspaces, documents, sharing, comments, version list and restore requests, uploads, collab tokens | `users`, `workspaces`, `memberships`, `documents`, `document_permissions`, `comments`, `audit_events` | REST/JSON `/v1/...` | Node 20+, TypeScript, Fastify | Postgres, Cognito, S3, Secrets Manager |\n| `collab` | Yjs sync, awareness (presence), persistence, compaction, auto-versions, read-only enforcement, revocation | `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots`, `doc_versions` | WSS (Yjs sync protocol + stateless JSON messages), `/healthz` | Node, Hocuspocus, Yjs | Postgres, Redis (M3), Secrets Manager |\n| `packages/doc-schema` | One definition of allowed document nodes and marks, plus `SCHEMA_VERSION` | none | npm workspace package | TipTap extensions | none |\n| Postgres | System of record | none | none | RDS Postgres 16, Multi-AZ, PITR | none |\n| Redis | Relays updates and awareness between `collab` instances. Not a store. | none | none | ElastiCache | Added in M3 |\n| Scheduled jobs | Hard-deletes expired documents, purges old versions | Only rows already marked for deletion | none | `api` image run as an ECS scheduled task | Postgres |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**`collab`, the core component.**\n- *Does not:* store metadata or comments, or make its own permission decisions beyond checking tokens and re-reading the ACL after a revocation.\n- *Interfaces:*\n  - WSS at `wss://collab.<domain>/`.\n  - The Yjs sync and awareness binary protocol, which is versioned by the library.\n  - Our own stateless JSON messages defined in `packages/protocol`, with a `v` field: `persisted {sv}`, `access-changed {role}`, `reload-required {reason}`.\n  - Expected load: up to 3,000 connections and up to about 1,000 merged writes per second (A2).\n- *Internals:*\n  - **Auth hook:** checks the JWT signature, expiry (5 min), that `doc_id` matches, and that `client_schema_version` is at least `documents.schema_version`. Viewers and commenters are marked read-only, so their sync updates are dropped and logged.\n  - **Load hook:** reads `doc_snapshots` and every row in `doc_updates` for the document, ordered by `seq`, and applies them.\n  - **Persistence extension:** described under Flow 2.\n  - **Compaction:** runs when there are 500 or more update rows, or when the document is unloaded, under a Postgres advisory lock.\n  - **Auto-version:** saves a full snapshot to `doc_versions` every 30 minutes of active editing.\n  - **Limits:** messages up to 1 MB; documents up to 10 MB, after which they turn read-only and raise an alert; 100 connections per document; at most 50 updates per second per connection. Every decode or apply is wrapped in try/catch, and a bad message closes the connection.\n- *Failure and recovery:* `collab` keeps no state that only it holds. If a task dies, clients reconnect through the ALB to any healthy task, which reloads from Postgres. The Yjs two-way state exchange then recovers any edits that weren't flushed (Flow 3). `/healthz` fails when the DB is unreachable or the event loop lag exceeds 200 ms.\n- *Scaling:* Scale out on connections or CPU. Redis relays updates and presence across instances (M3). Several instances may hold the same document, which is safe because log appends are idempotent (Section 8).\n\n**`api`.** Stateless Fastify service behind the ALB.\n- Every handler resolves the caller's role through one function, `authorize(user, doc, action)`.\n- Permission writes and `NOTIFY acl_changed` happen in the same transaction.\n- Version restore loads the old snapshot into a temporary Y.Doc, takes its ProseMirror JSON, and asks `collab`, through a stateless admin message on an internal-only path, to replace the content as one forward edit. History is never rewritten.\n- Failure: standard retries, with idempotency keys on POSTs that create things.\n\n**`web`.**\n- Local editing never waits on the network.\n- Keeps an IndexedDB copy per document.\n- The status indicator shows *Connected/Reconnecting/Offline* and *Saving…/Saved*. Saved means the server's `persisted.sv` covers this client's own Yjs `clientID` (Flow 2).\n- Warns on `beforeunload` if there are unsaved edits.\n- Handles `reload-required` by prompting the user to refresh.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n**Entities.** Every table carries `workspace_id` except `users`.\n\n| Table | Key columns | Writer | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `users` | id, oidc_sub (unique), email, name | api | Personal data: email and name |\n| `workspaces`, `memberships` | workspace_id, user_id, role | api | Tenant boundary |\n| `documents` | id, workspace_id, title, created_by, schema_version, deleted_at | api | Title is plain metadata, not edited collaboratively |\n| `document_permissions` | document_id, principal_type (user/workspace), principal_id, role | api | Index (principal_id, document_id) |\n| `doc_updates` | seq bigserial, document_id, update bytea, sv bytea, instance_id, contributor_ids uuid[], created_at | collab | Append-only. Index (document_id, seq). |\n| `doc_snapshots` | document_id PK, state bytea, compacted_at | collab | Current compacted state |\n| `doc_versions` | id, document_id, state bytea, created_at, created_by (null = auto), label | collab (auto), api (named labels) | Kept for 90 days, plus named versions |\n| `comments` | id, document_id, thread_id, author_id, body, anchor_from bytea, anchor_to bytea (Yjs relative positions), resolved_at | api | Plain-text body, at most 10k characters |\n| `audit_events` | actor, action, target, at | api, collab | Append-only |\n\n**Consistency.**\n- Document content is merged by the CRDT, so no transactions are needed across edits. Each `doc_updates` insert is atomic by itself.\n- Each instance writes the **diff of its in-memory document since its own last persisted state vector**. That diff includes edits it received from other instances, so the same content can appear in two rows. Applying a Yjs update twice changes nothing, so duplicates only cost storage, and compaction removes them.\n- **Compaction steps:** take an advisory lock on the document, read the snapshot and all update rows up to a maximum `seq` S, merge them, upsert the snapshot, and delete rows ≤ S, all in one transaction. Rows appended after S stay in place, which is correct because merge order doesn't matter.\n- **Permissions and metadata** are ordinary relational data with ordinary transactions.\n\n**Access patterns.**\n- Load a document: one snapshot plus fewer than 500 rows.\n- Hot write path: inserts on `doc_updates`, about 1 per second per actively edited document.\n- List documents: `document_permissions` joined to `documents` by principal.\n\n**Retention, deletion, backup.**\n- Soft delete, then hard delete of every row for the document after 30 days by the scheduled job.\n- Hard delete of a user's documents when their account is deleted.\n- RDS point-in-time recovery for 14 days, with a 5-minute recovery point for server-side storage loss and a 1-hour restore target.\n- After a restore, clients that were online push back newer edits automatically. That's a CRDT property, verified in M3.\n- One restore drill before beta.\n\n**Classification.**\n- Document content and comments are confidential. They are encrypted at rest (RDS KMS), **never logged**, and never included in metrics or error reports.\n- Email addresses are masked in logs.\n\n**Schema evolution.**\n- SQL changes are expand-then-contract (add, backfill, switch reads, remove) through `db/migrations`. CI runs them up and down.\n- **Document schema changes** (`packages/doc-schema`) are additive only. Readers ship one release before writers. `documents.schema_version` is raised only when new node types are first written, and the `collab` auth hook rejects older clients with `reload-required`. This handles H4.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**Flow 1: open a document and join the session**\n1. `web` calls `GET /v1/documents/:id`. `api` checks `authorize(view)` and returns metadata and the role.\n2. `web` calls `POST /v1/documents/:id/collab-token`. `api` returns a JWT signed with the Secrets Manager key, containing `{doc_id, user_id, role, workspace_id, exp: 5m}`.\n3. `web` loads the IndexedDB copy if one exists, so the content renders instantly. It then opens a WSS connection with the token and its `client_schema_version`.\n4. `collab` checks the token and schema version and sets read-only for viewers and commenters. It loads the document from memory, or from Postgres if it isn't loaded yet.\n5. Two-way sync exchange (each side sends what the other lacks), then presence starts. Remote cursors appear.\n\n**Flow 2: concurrent edits and \"Saved\"**\n1. Alice types. TipTap applies the change locally in under 16 ms. Yjs produces an update, which y-indexeddb stores and the provider sends.\n2. `collab` applies it and broadcasts to Bob, who sees it in under 250 ms. Each `collab` instance holding the document marks it as changed.\n3. Every 500 ms while changed, the instance captures `diff = encodeStateAsUpdate(doc, lastPersistedSV)` and `sv = encodeStateVector(doc)`, then inserts them into `doc_updates`.\n4. After the commit, it sends `persisted {sv}` to the document's connections.\n5. Alice's client compares `sv[myClientID]` with its own local clock. If the server has caught up, the indicator shows **Saved**.\n\n**Flow 3 (failure path): `collab` task crashes during typing**\n1. Alice's last 400 ms of edits were broadcast to Bob but not yet flushed when `collab-1` is killed. Alice still sees **Saving…**.\n2. The WebSocket closes, or a missed ping is detected within 30 s for half-open connections. The provider reconnects with 0.5–2 s jittered backoff through the ALB to `collab-2`. If the token has expired it fetches a new one first.\n3. `collab-2` loads from Postgres without the missing 400 ms. During the sync exchange, Alice's client sends the updates the server lacks, and so does Bob's.\n4. `collab-2` flushes and sends `persisted`. Alice sees **Saved**. Nothing is lost.\n5. The remaining exposure: Alice closes the tab *and* IndexedDB isn't available (private browsing) within that window, *and* no other editor received the edits. The `beforeunload` warning and the \"Saving…\" state make this visible. We accept this risk.\n6. Postgres unavailable: `collab` keeps editing in memory with retries, \"Saved\" stops advancing, an alert fires once the oldest unsaved change is more than 10 s old, and new document loads fail with a retryable error.\n\n**Flow 4: access revoked during an editing session**\n1. The owner downgrades Bob to viewer. `api` commits the permission change and `NOTIFY acl_changed {doc_id, user_id}` in one transaction.\n2. Every `collab` instance listening on that channel finds Bob's connections, re-reads his role from the DB, and switches them to read-only with `access-changed {role:viewer}`. If he has no access at all, it closes them with code 4403.\n3. Target: within 5 s. A backstop re-checks every connection's role every 10 minutes in case a notification is missed while an instance reconnects to the DB.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Options considered | Rationale (drivers) | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| D1 | Merge with **Yjs CRDT** | OT (ShareDB); Automerge; Yjs | Integrity: mature and widely used. Latency: merges locally. Offline: merges without a central server. Time to market: we don't implement the algorithm. OT needs a single ordering server per document and makes offline harder. | **Hard** (stored format) | S1 finds divergence or performance problems we can't fix |\n| D2 | **Build on OSS (Hocuspocus)** | Managed (Liveblocks, Tiptap Cloud); a custom server on y-protocols; Hocuspocus | Fits the team's stack. Already has auth and storage hooks and a Redis extension. No per-connection vendor cost. Data stays in our DB. Managed would save about 4–6 weeks but ties our content storage to a vendor. | Medium | S2 shows the hooks can't support the persisted-ack design (then write a custom server, +2–3 weeks), or the business prefers to buy |\n| D3 | **TipTap (ProseMirror)** editor | Lexical (+Yjs); Slate; TipTap | Strongest Yjs binding (y-prosemirror), a strict schema that helps H4, and a large extension ecosystem | **Hard** (schema shape) | S1 measures over 16 ms keystroke latency or a broken undo experience |\n| D4 | **Append-only update log + compacted snapshot in Postgres** | One blob overwritten on debounce; S3 objects; append-log | Integrity: safe with multiple writers and makes the persisted-ack possible. Uses the one DB the team knows. | Medium | Update row volume degrades DB p95, or total version storage passes about 100 GB (move snapshots and versions to S3) |\n| D5 | **Two deployables, `api` and `collab`** | One process; two | Availability: API releases don't drop editing sessions. Long-lived sockets scale differently from request/response. | Easy | Never mind |\n| D6 | **Redis relay between instances, any instance may hold a document** (M3) | Route each document to one instance with consistent hashing; Redis relay | Simpler routing. The ALB needs no affinity. D4 already makes multiple writers safe. | Medium | Redis relay latency pushes p95 past 250 ms, or very hot documents need affinity |\n| D7 | **Comments in Postgres via `api`, anchored with Yjs relative positions** | Comments inside the Y.Doc; Postgres | Access control: commenters never write to document content. Comments can be queried for notifications. | Medium | Comment anchoring breaks often during heavy concurrent editing |\n| D8 | **Versions as periodic full snapshots; restore as a forward edit** | Yjs snapshots with garbage collection off; full snapshots | Keeping garbage collection lets documents stay small. Restore doesn't rewrite history, so it's safe for live collaborators. | Medium | Users need per-keystroke history or blame |\n| D9 | **AWS ECS Fargate + RDS + Terraform + GitHub Actions** | Kubernetes; Fly/Render; ECS | Low operational load for 5 engineers, and managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery | Easy–medium | The organisation already runs a different platform |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n- **Security (M1 skeleton, M2 complete, M4 review).**\n  - Cognito OIDC, with the session in an httpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie.\n  - Collab JWTs last 5 minutes and are signed with a key from Secrets Manager, rotated quarterly with a two-key overlap.\n  - Every query includes `workspace_id`.\n  - Threats and mitigations:\n    1. *Connecting to a document you can't access:* token tied to `doc_id`, tested in the auth test matrix.\n    2. *A viewer sending edits from a modified client:* server-side read-only enforcement plus an audit event.\n    3. *Malformed or oversized updates crashing or flooding `collab`:* size, rate and connection caps, try/catch, and a fuzz test feeding random bytes into the decoder.\n    4. *XSS through content or links:* rendering only through the ProseMirror schema, an `http/https/mailto` allowlist for link targets, a strict CSP, and images served only from our CloudFront host.\n    5. *Cross-tenant leaks:* authorisation tests on every endpoint and role.\n  - Dependency scanning (`pnpm audit` plus Dependabot) and image scanning (ECR) run in CI.\n- **Reliability (M1–M3).**\n  - Targets are in Section 3.\n  - Multi-AZ RDS. At least two tasks each for `api` and `collab`.\n  - Reconnect uses jittered exponential backoff capped at 10 s, which prevents a stampede after a deploy.\n  - Persistence retries with backoff and alerts.\n  - Idempotency comes from the CRDT for content and from idempotency keys for REST creates.\n- **Observability (M1 baseline, M3 alerts and dashboards).**\n  - pino JSON logs with `conn_id`, `doc_id` and `user_id`, never content.\n  - OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch: `ws_connections`, `docs_loaded`, `update_apply_ms`, `persist_flush_ms`, `unpersisted_age_seconds`, `reconnects_total`, `readonly_rejects_total`, `acl_revoke_latency_ms`.\n  - A **synthetic probe** of two headless Yjs clients editing a canary document every minute measures propagation p95 and the full save cycle.\n  - Alerts, each linked to a runbook in `docs/runbooks/`:\n    - `unpersisted_age_seconds` over 10 s;\n    - probe p95 over 500 ms for 10 minutes;\n    - probe failing to save;\n    - `collab` healthy tasks fewer than 2.\n- **Performance and capacity (M3).**\n  - Expected bottlenecks: Node event loop on hot documents, DB insert rate, and memory (about 1,000 documents × roughly 1 MB in memory, so 2 GB tasks).\n  - `tests/load` is a Node generator driving real Yjs clients. It runs from ECS at 2× A2: 6,000 connections, 2,000 documents, 20 editors on 10 hot documents.\n- **Cost.** Roughly $600–1,000/month for prod plus staging at beta: RDS Multi-AZ about $250–400, Fargate about $150–250, ElastiCache about $50–100, ALB, CloudFront and CloudWatch about $100. Main drivers are RDS size and IOPS from `doc_updates`. Controls: AWS Budgets alerts at 80%, cost-allocation tags per environment, and the compaction threshold.\n- **Operations (M4).** The team owns on-call through business-hours paging during beta, with runbooks for: DB failover, `collab` crash loop, stuck compaction, a document exceeding the size cap, rotating the token key, and restoring a document from a version or point-in-time recovery.\n- **AI-specific concerns.** Not applicable. There are no AI components in scope.\n\n## 12. Build Sequence\n\nTeam assumption: 5 engineers (2 frontend-leaning, 2 backend, 1 backend/infra). Sizes are rough guides, not commitments. The other sections are short but complete.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** A browser-based rich-text editor where business teams edit the same document at the same time. It shows live cursors, has sharing permissions, comments and version history, and keeps working through short network drops. Think of a focused Google Docs for teams (A1).\n- **Shape:** A React and TipTap editor in the browser. A **`collab`** WebSocket service, built on the open-source Yjs ecosystem (Hocuspocus), merges and relays edits. A separate **`api`** service handles login, documents, sharing and comments. Both store data in one Postgres database. Everything runs on AWS ECS Fargate.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Edits are merged with a **CRDT (Yjs)**, not operational transformation. A CRDT is a data structure that lets copies edited separately merge automatically and end up identical.\n  2. We build on **open-source Yjs, TipTap and Hocuspocus** instead of buying a managed collaboration service or writing a sync server from scratch.\n  3. Documents are stored as an **append-only log of updates plus a compacted snapshot in Postgres**. Multiple servers can write to it safely.\n  4. **\"Saved\" is a real guarantee.** The server tells each client which of its edits are committed to the database.\n  5. **Two deployables, `api` and `collab`,** so that releasing the API doesn't disconnect everyone who is editing.\n- **First milestone (about 4–5 weeks):** Two people log in and edit the same document in a deployed staging environment. Their edits survive a server crash. Three time-boxed spikes run in parallel: editor binding and merge correctness, the durability and \"Saved\" guarantee, and WebSocket behaviour on AWS.\n- **Top risks:**\n  - Silent data loss or copies that drift apart. This is the worst outcome possible.\n  - Changes to the document schema deleting content on older clients.\n  - Permission checks being skipped on the WebSocket path.\n  - The team's lack of CRDT experience slowing everything down.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Teams now draft in files they email around or in tools that lock a document to one editor. Concurrent edits collide or overwrite each other, and nobody can trust which copy is current.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Several people edit one document at once and see each other's changes in under 250 ms.\n  - No edit the UI reported as saved is ever lost.\n  - Access control is enforced on every path.\n  - Private beta in about 16 weeks (A5).\n- **Non-goals for beta:** spreadsheets and slides, native mobile apps, full offline-first use (creating or browsing documents offline), suggestion or track-changes mode, public link sharing, SAML/SCIM, import and export, search, AI features, multi-region, end-to-end encryption.\n- **Success measures:**\n  - At least 5 beta workspaces active weekly.\n  - Zero confirmed lost-edit incidents.\n  - p95 time for an edit to reach other editors under 250 ms, measured in production by a synthetic probe.\n  - At least 99.9% of minutes with the editing service available.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | **Data integrity** | (a) All clients and the stored copy are byte-identical after merging, with 0 drift across 10,000 fuzz runs per night. (b) Recovery point is zero for any edit the UI showed as \"Saved\". (c) \"Saved\" appears within 2 s at p95 after typing stops. *(Assumption)* | Losing someone's writing destroys trust and can't be repaired afterwards. |\n| 2 | **Access-control correctness** | No read or write without permission, checked on HTTP and WebSocket paths. Revoked access takes effect on live sessions within 5 s. *(Assumption)* | Documents hold business-confidential content (A6). |\n| 3 | **Collaboration latency** | Local keystroke to screen under 16 ms and never waits on the network. Remote edit propagation under 250 ms p95 in-region, for documents with up to 20 editors. *(Assumption)* | This is what makes it feel \"real-time\". |\n| 4 | **Time to market** | Private beta in about 16 weeks with 5 engineers (A3, A5). | Rules out building merge algorithms from scratch. |\n| 5 | **Availability** | Editing available 99.9% monthly. A deploy or crash causes at most about 5 s of reconnecting and loses no edits. If `collab` goes down, users keep typing locally. *(Assumption)* | A CRDT lets us trade server uptime for client resilience. |\n\nCost comes after these. The target is under about $1,000/month at beta scale *(assumption)*.\n\n**Key functional requirements that shape the structure:**\n- Rich text: headings, lists, bold/italic/code, links, images, block quotes. Tables are a stretch goal.\n- Live presence and cursors.\n- Per-document roles: owner, editor, commenter, viewer.\n- Comments anchored to text.\n- Version history with restore.\n- Edits made during a disconnect sync when the connection returns.\n\n**Constraints (all assumed):**\n- 5 engineers who are strong in TypeScript, React, Node and Postgres, with no CRDT experience (A3).\n- AWS, single region (A4).\n- No regulated data (A6).\n- Managed OIDC identity (A8).\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n| Hard part | Why it's hard |\n|---|---|\n| H1. Merge correctness and editor binding | New to the team. Bugs show up as rare divergence that is hard to reproduce. |\n| H2. Durability and \"Saved\" semantics | Yjs servers usually persist on a debounce, so a crash can lose the last few seconds unless the design closes that gap. |\n| H3. Authorisation on long-lived WebSockets | Permissions change while connections stay open. Viewers must not be able to send edits even from a modified client. |\n| H4. Document schema evolution | The document format is effectively permanent. y-prosemirror can **delete** content it can't map to an older client's schema *(to verify in S1)*. |\n| H5. Running more than one `collab` instance | Fan-out between instances, multiple writers to the same document, compaction, and reconnect storms during deploys. |\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nThe workspace is empty: no code, infrastructure, CI or data. No organisational platform, mandated vendors or existing identity provider were mentioned, so the plan uses AWS and managed services (A4, A8). It proposes this repository layout:\n\n```\napps/web            React + Vite + TipTap client\napps/api            Fastify HTTP API\napps/collab         Hocuspocus WebSocket server\npackages/doc-schema shared TipTap/ProseMirror schema + schema_version (used by web AND collab)\npackages/protocol   shared types: collab-token claims, stateless message types\ndb/migrations       SQL migrations (node-pg-migrate)\ninfra/terraform     modules/ + envs/staging, envs/prod\ntests/fuzz, tests/e2e (Playwright), tests/load\ndocs/adr            decision records\n```\n\n## 5.
